transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Jared Klein (Stonebrook Head of Infra), Maya Patel (Stonebrook SecOps), Ethan Lu (SRE)

Summary: quick intro, confirm security/regional constraints, dig into private connectivity options (VPC peering vs private endpoints), discuss transit/gateway architecture and egress IPs, agree next steps for pilot and benchmarks. Lots of talk about SOC2, KMS/HSM, and regional gating.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Jared (Stonebrook): okay everybody, thanks for joining. we have about 50 minutes, i've got Maya and Ethan on the call as well. main thing is we need to understand how Redwood would actually sit inside our VPCs and what the onramp looks like.
00:12 Alyssa (Redwood AE): great, thanks Jared. quick intros — i'm Alyssa, i'll be your AE; Marco is our solutions engineer. can you give a tiny bit of context on what you run today and why private is on the table?
00:24 Jared: sure, we operate HR/finance models and customer PII, so we need the data plane to never touch public internet, and we also have strict region residency — EU for certain customers, US for others. latency target is sub-120ms p95 for short prompts, throughput varies.
00:42 Maya: and security reqs — SOC2 is tablestake, we do SAML SSO, RBAC enforced, and we require KMS-backed key management for any data at rest. we also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
00:55 Marco (Redwood SE): understood. Architecturally, Redwood Private can be deployed into a dedicated VPC per customer, or we can do a private endpoint model where you peer to our private subnet; there are tradeoffs. quick note, i might mangle some product names on the fly — sorry if i call the private onramp the "nexus" sometimes, that's an internal shorthand.
01:12 Ethan (SRE): that's fine. can you walk us through networking options? specifically interested in peering, transit gateway, and private endpoint (privatelink-ish) options.
01:22 Marco: yeah. option A: VPC peering between your VPC and the Redwood-managed inference VPC. low latency, simple route table changes, but peering scales poorly if you have dozens of VPCs. option B: Attach via transit gateway — we can peer to your transit for multi-VPC architectures. option C: Private endpoints aka privatelink — we expose an ENI in your subnet that routes to our infra; that handles egress and avoids full routing.
01:45 Jared: do you support regional restrictions? like we want EU models to stay in eu-west-1 only.
01:50 Marco: yes, we can pin models and routing policies by region. for Private deployments, the control plane is separate and we can enforce region gating; some customers run separate Redwood fleets per region. there is a small ops overhead but it's doable.
02:05 Maya: how are keys handled — does Redwood hold keys? we require customer-managed keys (CMK) in our KMS/HSM.
02:12 Marco: we support KMS integrations so you can hold CMKs; we support AWS KMS and external HSMs via standard integrations. again, i'll follow up with the exact attestation docs. sometimes our transcripts mix up the exact HSM vendor names — i'll send the security sheet.
02:27 Alyssa: quick question on egress — do you provide deterministic static outgoing IPs for callbacks and webhooks?
02:33 Marco: yes we can reserve egress IP blocks, typically as NAT egress from a set of managed NAT gateways/egress bridges. we call them egress slices internally; they can be whitelisted. note there's a small charge for static egress pools.
02:48 Ethan: our policy also restricts DNS resolution — we need to know if Redwood will create private hosted zones or if we must manage DNS records.
02:55 Marco: for private endpoints we can populate private hosted zones on your account, or you can point to the ENI IPs directly. both are supported. sometimes the auto-DNS gets noisy, so ops teams prefer the explicit records.
03:10 Jared: okay on scaling — our load profile is about 50 rps steady, with peaks up to 200 rps for batch windows. what sizing and GPU footprint would that map to?
03:22 Marco: initial, rough guess — for a large 8k context model, 50 rps steady might be a couple of reserved cards in a dedicated pool; for burst to 200 you'd want autoscaling with a burst buffer. i'll produce a capacity estimate after we get a sample prompt distribution and token rates.
03:38 Maya: are there any compliance blockers for us running the control plane outside our VPC? we prefer control plane in Redwood but data plane inside our VPC.
03:46 Marco: that's a common pattern. our control plane handles orchestration but metadata can be scrubbed; we support private control plane options for high-compliance customers. we also provide audit logs and can forward them to your SIEM over TLS.
04:02 Jared: what about KV cache / context caching — we have some long-running chat sessions and it's important that the caching stays low-latency and doesn't traverse public internet.
04:12 Marco: our runtime keeps the KV cache local to the inference pods; with private deployment it'll remain in your VPC/per-customer fleet. there was an internal note i always butcher into saying "K V cache" but yes it's local.
04:24 Ethan: any constraints on VPC CIDR sizes or route table limits we should be aware of?
04:30 Marco: Peering: route table entries scale linearly, so if you use peering across many VPCs you'll hit route counts. transit gateway is recommended for many VPCs. private endpoints avoid route explosion. also need to consider ENI limits per AZ for privatelink.
04:46 Maya: outbound TLS interception — we have some proxies that do TLS termination for inspection. will that break anything?
04:52 Marco: if you terminate TLS and re-encrypt, it's fine as long as mutual TLS or SNI/pinned certs are configured. for model payloads we still recommend end-to-end encryption to avoid man-in-the-middle altering content.
05:08 Alyssa: quick note — some customers ask about dedicated capacity vs hosted. any initial thoughts on preference?
05:14 Jared: for us, we'd prefer private because of data residency and egress controls. dedicated might be an option if we want predictable throughput without managing networking.
05:24 Marco: yep, dedicated is more about reserved GPU pools, private is about where the network and data plane reside. you can have both — a private, dedicated fleet.
05:34 Ethan: curious about rollback/fallback — if a region has a partial outage, can requests failover to another region without violating residency?
05:43 Marco: we have routing policies — automatic fallback can be enabled but that would cross-region. for strict residency you can set failover to manual or to a compatible model within the same region. we can also do read-only replica caches in other regions depending on your risk appetite.
05:59 Maya: on authentication, do you support SSO and role-based access for the console and API keys?
06:05 Marco: yes — SAML/SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC. API keys are scoped and tokens can be rotated; we also support short-lived credentials via our integration.
06:16 Jared: what about billing and network egress charges — will we see AWS egress billed to our account or Redwood's?
06:24 Alyssa: typically egress from our managed VPC is billed on the Redwood invoice as part of the dedicated/private add-on, but if you attach to our systems via privatelink in your account you can choose to keep egress on your cloud bill. we'll show options in pricing.
06:42 Ethan: any gotchas with on-prem or air-gapped options? we might have teams that want an appliance.
06:47 Marco: we offer an on-prem package for fully air-gapped customers; it's heavier ops but doable. usually that triggers an enterprise contract. i'll include the on-prem checklist in the follow-up.
06:58 Maya: okay, operationally — we need audit log format examples and how long logs are retained.
07:05 Alyssa: we'll send the log retention matrix. typical retention is 90 days in the console, longer if you buy add-on. we can forward logs to your S3 or SIEM.
07:15 Jared: I want to call out that we need static egress IPs for incoming webhooks to our downstream systems. you said you can provide those?
07:21 Marco: yes, static egress IPs are supported. you'll get a small pool maybe /28 depending on scale.
07:28 Ethan: latency testing — can we run a test from our VPC into the Redwood private endpoint to measure p95?
07:34 Marco: absolutely. i'll prepare a small benchmark harness and a script you can run from an EC2 in your VPC that hits the private endpoint. it'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token throughput.
07:44 Maya: can you also include an example of the network ACL and security group rules we'll need?
07:49 Marco: yes, sample SG/ACL templates will be included.
07:52 Alyssa: any other blockers we should surface now?
07:55 Jared: just timeline — we need a pilot by end of April; if we can get pilot infra up in two weeks, that helps.
08:03 Marco: that's feasible. i'll prioritize the benchmark and the capacity estimate.
08:08 Alyssa: recap and next steps: i'll send SOC2 and security pack; Marco will send bench script, capacity estimate, and SG/ACL examples; Maya to share egress whitelist and contact for SIEM ingestion. then we schedule a pilot kickoff.
08:23 Jared: sounds good. thanks all.

(End of recording)
